_about: Free play ('open history'). The war starts as it did on 1 September 1939 and after that no computer-run nation follows history's plan: each one's staff weighs up its fronts every month and decides for itself. 'temper' is national character: attackAt is the strength ratio (our attack against their defence near the front, forts, terrain and season counted) at which a staff opens an offensive, persist the ratio below which it calls one off, minOdds the odds a single attack needs. A nation with no attackAt never opens an offensive of its own, though it still defends and counter-attacks. 'mood' is how far a nation's nerve differs from one war to the next (each war draws its own, by seed). The staff's habits: an offensive that gains no ground for 'stall' months is called off unless the odds are still good, and the army then rests 'rest' months before it tries again. A front that can only be attacked head-on into fortifications counts 'headOn' times as strong. An offensive under way keeps up to 'commit' times the enemy's strength for itself, so that a second one is not opened with the same troops. A front is a serious one when the enemy's strength on it is at least 'major' of this nation's whole army. Each month's attacks are bounded: the main thrust goes along the easiest road to the nearest enemy capital, 'thrust' regions deep ([opening month of a nation that makes war by speed, any other month]) with the ground on either side, and elsewhere only prizes, bulges in the line and places held by no more than 'weak' divisions are attacked. The road starts only where the army has at least 'foothold' of the force it has at its strongest point. At a ratio of 'general' or more the whole of the enemy's front is pressed. A side-show is taken on to a depth of 'bound' regions, a theatre overseas 'boundOverseas'. With the enemy within 'guardWithin' regions of the capital, 'guard' corps are kept in it. 'ops' are the great decisions history took, written as choices: a staff may take one up when its conditions hold (the 'if' list reads as in diplomacy.json, plus 'quiet' for no serious land front, 'collapsing:FRA,0.07' and 'month:5,6,7'), the months of the war lie between 'from' and 'to', the odds in prospect are at least 'ratio', and the month's draw comes in under 'chance'. It then spends 'prep' months bringing the army up before it declares war on the 'declare' list, and attacks for at least 'push' months. 'season' lists the months of the year, numbered from 1 for January, in which it may begin. A 'side' operation needs no build-up and does not take the main army: a landing, or a small neighbour. 'join' moves a neutral onto that side of the alignment track when it marches. 'staging' is a force kept ready for the operation until it is launched, and 'landings' name the corps that go by sea and the shores each one tries in turn.

impatience._about: A war nobody is fighting makes bolder generals. 'after' is months without a land battle between a nation and the enemies on a front (or since their war began): past the first term a staff opens an offensive at 'ratio'[0] of the strength ratio it would usually wait for, past the second at 'ratio'[1], but never below 'floor'. A nation with no attackAt of its own opens one past the last term if the ratio reaches 'any'. A main effort opened this way runs for 'effort' months before anyone asks what it has gained, and for those months single attacks go in at 'odds' (shorter than the nation's minOdds). A staff that stays on the defensive still makes local attacks once the first term has gone by: up to 'locals' a month, each at odds of 'local'[0] or better (past the second term, 'local'[1]), and it keeps at them while the last one is no more than 'effort' months old.

coast._about: The coast watch. A computer staff at war with an enemy who has sea lift, and whose home army is not already fighting it on land, expects him by sea once the two have not fought for a season, and for a year after: it keeps a corps of its field army (two divisions or more: a town's standing garrison does not count) in each harbour of its own homeland that his ships can reach within a landing's range, from the ports he holds or an ally's where his troops stand, the most valuable first, up to 'share' of its corps in the field (never fewer than 'least') and 'each' to a harbour, and its treasury raises fortifications there to level 'works'. Conquered coasts are not watched. 'dig': a computer staff that can raise no corps for want of men puts idle money into fortifications in the provinces of its homeland nearest the enemy that he does not yet stand next to, 'orders' a month, to level 'top' (the capital to 'capital'), keeping 'keep' in the treasury.

descent._about: The second front. A nation with sea lift that has been at war with an enemy for 'after' months with no land battle against him and no troops of its home army in touch with ground he holds keeps 'force' corps by a quay (a home port with a lane open to his harbours) and crosses the sea: to a harbour of his that is unguarded, or guarded at 'odds' or better, with a crossing no riskier than 'risk' and no more than 'near' times its own strength within a march of the beach. It tries in a month with chance 'chance', and waits 'every' months after a landing. The staff names the beach it has its eye on a month ahead: its fleet then covers the crossing and its fighters fight for the sky over the beach, and a beach they cannot open in half a year is given up for a year. The men it puts ashore stay there, and while they are fewer than 'hold' divisions, or than 'feed' times the enemy army next to their ground, every ship it has carries more to them each month: into a harbour in friendly hands, or over the beach while the harbour town still holds out. An army standing idle on a far shore (friendly ground away from home with no enemy on it or next to it) does the same from a port there, against an enemy it has not fought for 'abroad' months. A staff heeds its own forecast ('heed'): it lands no force on a beach where the sea behind could be closed and the force cut off from its supplies (the same forecast a player reads on the landing card, navy.ts). 'mainland' is that rule for a first landing on a shore with a land frontier; 'island' is the same for a landing that takes a whole island (a province with no land frontier), and it is off: in the wars measured (Version 75) landings of that kind under a warning mostly held and cost few men, and the island war to come would be forbidden by it; 'wave' is the rule for a further wave sent over the beach to men already ashore. A player may still order any such landing by hand. The hardest level has rules of its own for the player's coasts (difficulty.json). 'planned' holds history's shores for the staffs that have such a list (Version 77, the design director's rulings 39 and 40): 'open' names the countries on whose own shores the staff may open a second front by a landing of its own, 'join' those on whose ground it goes by ship to a front its side already holds; colonies and islands overseas are open to it always. Such a staff does not go elsewhere because elsewhere is clear: where its shores are barred it names its beach, its fleet and its fighters work on the crossing, and it waits. 'with' is the build-up: the staff opens no front of its own on a mainland until this many of its field corps stand across the ocean (9 for the United States: the landing force and two more to follow it in; with none, three corps put ashore at Bordeaux in the autumn of 1942 were destroyed by the spring in most wars). An island taken whole and a colony overseas need no such army, and joining a front its side already holds never waits for it. The United States opens on France and Italy (with North Africa, its landings in the real war) and joins a front in the west or in Italy; Canada and Brazil open no front of their own on a mainland and join their allies' (Canada in the west and in Italy, Brazil in Italy and France); a staff with no list goes where it judges best, and at the stop of the history dial where nobody has read the books so does every staff. History's dates (Version 79, ruling 60), at every stop but the two loosest: 'from' gives a mainland shore the month a staff's own landing may first be made there (the Italian mainland July 1943, France May 1944, Greece October 1944 for Britain), after which the build-up and the forecast still decide; islands and colonies are open always, and under 'lapse' France's date is set aside for as long as an enemy of Germany's stands on German home ground. A province under 'not' is no part of a list whoever owns it (Albania is not the Italian mainland). They bind a computer staff opening a front of its own, never a player and never the joining of a front already held. Britain's list ('book': kept only at the stops where the dates hold) is the Italian mainland, France and Greece: not Norway, Denmark or Albania. Canada's corps are the island's guard ('base': they are shipped to Britain's own harbours and nowhere else): at those stops they go on to the continent not before 'joinFrom' (January 1943), and only behind a British or American army ('behind'): into its landing, a harbour it holds, or one with its field corps in it or next to it. 'front' is how near the enemy must be, in marches over ground its side holds, for a harbour an ally holds to count as a front that an army across an ocean is shipped to (world.json 'overseas'): not only the harbour of a landing still in the lander's own hands, but one handed back to the country it was freed for, one reached overland, or an ally's own that the war has come to. 'door' names the staffs with their capital beyond the old chart for whom an enemy whose home is on their own side of the ocean is the first business (Version 81, the design director's rulings 75 and 76; the United States): on that side of the water such a staff has no list of shores and no build-up figure, it does not wait the quiet year, its landing force is brought to the quay by rail at once and is no part of the army shipped across the ocean while he stands, it lands the month the force is ready (no 'chance'), by a landing within a landing's range of its own home harbours under every test of the landing card, and when he is beaten the force takes ship for home. Beyond that range nothing is changed, and a player's country is never moved by it. 'strength' is the test of strength (Version 83, the design director's rulings 89, 92 and 94; ashore.ts): before a computer staff puts a force across the sea, onto a held coast or into a friendly harbour, it reckons what the defender can bring to that place within 'months' and what it will have there itself, and sails only where its chance of being still ashore after them is 'sure' or better ('bold' for a staff of bold character; none sails on less than 'even'). The defender's side of it is his field corps within that many marches of the place by land (one in the line against an army farther off counts for 'line' of its strength) and 'reserve' of his corps farther off, out of the line, on ground of his in one piece with ground he holds within those marches, which his railways can bring ('door' of them where his own home country lies within those marches of the place and is still his: in the wars measured half of Germany's free corps came down on a harbour of northern Italy within two months, a fifth on a beach in France); a harbour more than that many marches from any ground of his is out of his reach and passes. The staff's own side is the force as it would defend the place, the corps of its side already within those marches, and the corps standing ready at the quay, or a march from it on quiet ground of its side, that its ships can bring in after it within the time. Where its usual force does not pass, a staff sends a bigger first wave, as many as its ships lift and the quay holds, up to 'wave'; or it builds up and waits; or it takes a beach that passes (a mainland beach refused for want of strength comes before an island or a colony that passes: for 'every' months the staff builds up for the mainland sooner than spend its force on the lesser prize). History's dates come first at the stops where they hold, and the test second. 'first' is the main front (ruling 98): for the staffs named in 'for', among the harbours of a front their side holds that pass the test, one on the home ground of a country named in 'ground' comes before every other, a harbour gained by a treaty among them. A staff that waits behind its allies (Canada) goes, at the stops where history's dates do not hold, only into a landing of theirs that passes this test as it stands. A player is never held to it: his landing card shows the same reckoning as one more line, on what his side knows.
